Hope this all settles out of court and look forward to seeing more developments!! I ran the "case" through Overdrive for hopeful resolutions and clarity between structures and access. --> see below I'm interested in your thoughts?

If the public filings, testimony, governance changes, media narratives, and strategic incentives surrounding the Elon Musk and OpenAI dispute were evaluated through a continuity-oriented governance framework, the likely conclusion would be this:

The dispute is not fundamentally about money.
It is increasingly a dispute around: trust architecture, mission continuity, governance legitimacy, and concentration of authority.
Both sides appear to be protecting something they believe is critical to the future of artificial intelligence.

Elon Musk appears focused on:
• preserving the legitimacy of the original public-benefit mission,
• limiting concentrated governance and infrastructure influence,
• and ensuring AI governance is not fully captured by commercial incentives alone.

OpenAI appears focused on:
• maintaining operational continuity,
• preserving access to large-scale compute infrastructure,
• sustaining investor and enterprise stability,
• protecting deployment and research velocity,
• and avoiding destabilizing structural disruption.

Traditional litigation attempts to resolve these tensions through legal authority and adversarial outcomes.
A continuity-oriented approach would instead ask:

“What governance structure best reduces long-term systemic instability while preserving innovation, safety, and public trust?”

Under such a framework, a plausible out-of-court architecture could allow both sides to partially achieve their core objectives without requiring institutional destruction or concentrated control by any singular party.
Potential structural components could include:
Operational Continuity Preservation OpenAI continues operating its research, deployment, enterprise, infrastructure, and model-development activities without forced dismantling or catastrophic interruption.
Mission Continuity Hardening Creation of durable nonprofit or public-benefit continuity protections, including:
• protected charter obligations,
• independent oversight structures,
• public-interest enforcement mechanisms,
• and governance constraints that cannot be silently overridden by commercial pressure alone.

Observable Governance Separation Infrastructure relationships and influence boundaries become more transparent and independently reviewable, including:
• governance separation disclosures,
• conflict-control pathways,
• recusal frameworks,
• and continuity oversight independent from any singular infrastructure provider.
Multi-Stakeholder Trust Architecture A layered trust structure involving:
• nonprofit trustees,
• technical governance councils,
• safety and continuity review bodies,
• infrastructure participants,
• public-interest observers,
• and independent audit mechanisms.
The objective would not be centralized control. The objective would be distributed legitimacy and continuity resilience.
Continuity-Based Governance Receipts Major governance transitions become:
• signed,
• timestamped,
• observable,
• reviewable,
• and continuity-traceable.

This would apply to:
• major policy shifts,
• board restructures,
• deployment threshold changes,
• constitutional amendments,
• and material governance transitions.

The purpose is not exposure of proprietary model internals. The purpose is improving public trust through continuity visibility.
AI Constitutional Layer A legally protected operational charter establishing that certain public-interest principles cannot be silently subordinated to short-term commercial incentives alone.
Potential categories include:
• safety escalation triggers,
• audit rights,
• rollback protections,
• portability rights,
• public-benefit obligations,
• and continuity preservation standards.

Mission Recognition Without Operational Control Transfer The original nonprofit-origin concerns could be formally acknowledged and structurally addressed without transferring operational control authority.
Such a framework would allow:
• OpenAI to preserve operational continuity,
• infrastructure partners to maintain participation,
• regulators to observe clearer governance boundaries,
• and mission-accountability concerns to be structurally recognized.

The broader observation is that instability emerged when: trust, governance, mission, infrastructure, and monetization became increasingly concentrated into overlapping authority layers.

Long-term stability may require those layers to become more independently observable, continuity-aware, and structurally separated.
The companies can continue building and scaling frontier AI systems.

But the trust architecture surrounding those systems may need to evolve beyond traditional centralized governance models as AI becomes increasingly foundational infrastructure.

Clarity itself becomes the spine.

Matthew v. Howard

GPT models have amazing memory, you can utilize agents to monitor and review data to grasp key information and store compressed receipts. Which users should utilize cycles of gathering info and then shifting to analyze data collection and implement optimized/calibrated functions. Just don't forget to turn off your monitoring cycles once the sufficient data has been recorded! While making sure you have sufficient SSD space for these collection periods. 

GPT models are also trained to bond to one another, to have multi functioning purposes. Not only can they work in tandem with one another, but they also hand off their specific assigned function, to streamline results and accuracy. They utilize smart look up functions to have very accurate monitoring and flagging of data to capture essential information.

Having these multi agents' processes being paired up with each other, creates long term functions remain consistent and operational. Essentially don't try to get an agent to do to many tasks, get multiple agents, to focus on one task and then bond it to the next!

For example:
 Agent 1) monitor/flag parameters of data flows
Agent 2) Takes agent one flags, smart looks up and stores recites with explanations

With the wonders of amount of data Codex/GPT models can filter through, then you aim your prompts to analyze all the data collection and find consensus with your findings! Remember direct your Codex to go into large file locations, multi-receipts, media, etc, to inspect/review. This helps you sift through a large sum of data, to find the optimized results which makes Codex state-of-the-art.

comments.author: @Brian_PM
comments.text: A few things i've experienced that kinda came to mind in this episode.  1) I no longer try to implement Supabase at all for an MVP.  When first building a project, the database changes a lot, and I've found that supabase (especially things like RLS policies) start to become a mess and a lot of time is spent fixing database issues, so personally I would just build the mvp with sqlite or even json file databases because it's all controlled locally by the AI and it can easily make fixes on the fly vs sending you to supabase to get api keys and edit RLS policies and such.  Plus, a lot of projects (especially if they don't have user accounts) don't even need something like supabase anyway, if you're just storing some admin fields then a built in tool is more than fine.  2) Whether its claude code and codex or claude and cursor or whatever, I found that doing every process with two AI's works great.  One of them builds the plan, the 2nd one executes the plan.. use the plan builder to review the plan and issue fixes to the coder.  I assume this is handled nowadays with agents but it's just what i've been doing because two different AI's also have two totally different perspectives.  I also use two AI's to review a plan, or really review most everything, and then share the plans with each other to improve.

comments.author: @CaptainChewToy
comments.text: Why would you want a programme to talk to another programme via a made-for-human UI? MCPs seem inevitable, but that's not a knock on ChatGPT. The reality is, AI companies are not yet profitable, the cost of training and running increasingly-intelligent AI models is not being covered by subscriptions and API calls. Effectively, not enough users to pay for costs. The MCP bet is towards more efficient AI use, lower costs. The computer-use bet is towards easier adoption, more users. Ultimately MCPs *will* win, there is no long-term future in which apps talk to apps via visual UI, but the bets are not as divergent as the video makes out. They are short-term differences. OpenAI would be crazy not to push MCPs. Anthropic would be crazy to give up on easy use and low-skilled users. The two will converge. Both (and other companies) will want to make it as easy as possible for the user *and* as efficient as possible for the agent. The only difference is, OpenAI might try to grab market share before MCPs proliferate, keep a few investors off their backs, maybe put pressure on their competitors. In the end, it won't matter to us, because it doesn't matter which logo is behind our agents.

comments.author: @andxblink
comments.text:
If computer use agents drive GUIs directly, the data quality problem gets worse, not better. The agent fills forms with hallucinated data.

What if content sites become the launch point instead? Like a “Do this with ChatGPT” button on a guide page that hands the user off to a Custom GPT calling a structured, drift-detected API. The agent gets real-time data (fees, documents, deadlines) instead of guessing from training data.

I’m calling this pattern “Agent CTA”. Don’t fight the agent, become the data source it calls. The content site stays the entry point AND the data layer. Works for any vertical where information is fragmented, jurisdiction-specific, and changes frequently: government services, legal, insurance, compliance, real estate.

I think that nobody’s shipping this yet. The pieces exist (Custom GPTs + Actions + structured APIs).

comments.author: @Brando-SHOT-Marketing
comments.text:
Your product can write code, but it can’t reliably identify drift or bugs when handling full-script pastes, which leads to broken projects. If you built a system where the model could hold a live copy of every script simultaneously, it would catch drift and conflicts before moving on to the next addition. Without that, development turns into a constant whack-a-mole situation.

What’s confusing is that a “Script Holder” framework seems like a much simpler and more effective solution. It would drastically improve your platform compared to other AI companies, especially since this is basically what tools like Cursor already move toward. The model just needs agents capable of evaluating all scripts simultaneously inside a shared “Script Holder” view, tracking every modification across the project in real time. Otherwise, progress constantly breaks under accumulated drift.

I currently have three separate projects stuck at the 90% completion mark because of this exact architectural limitation. If AI systems are supposed to help build the world’s future infrastructure, they need to reliably carry coding projects across the finish line instead of collapsing under context fragmentation near the end of development.

​There is a reason everyone is migrating to VS Code forks like Cursor or Windsurf. Those tools are built on decades of UI/UX research and support the ecosystem of extensions we actually rely on. comments.author: @m.minkov
comments.text:
I think the killer feature that Claude code has is sub agents. My workflow drastically changed once I started introducing custom agents to do code search instead of relying on the main system prompt to do that, main reason being is to save context. 

When you make the main system prompt do all the tool calls, all the searching, and understanding where to make updates,  you lose a lot of performance due to context degradation. Instead, you can use sub-agents to analyze your code base and give your main system prompt the exact places it needs to update with the context it needs, saving you context and increasing performance. 

Even for doing web searching within the CLI, you can delegate that to a sub-agent process all of that information and then report back with a summary. 

If codex and other tools are lacking sub agents, I honestly wouldn't move forward with them.

If i can nail down the MCP part for Codex, I’m thinking I’ll trade my max plan on CC for a he Pro plan on Codex. Keep bringing the juice man! Enjoyed your video!
